To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the nationalizing states of post-communist Eurasia have not, in general, been ‘successful’ in their efforts to become nation-states; (b) the nationalizing projects of these states have been shaped by the legacies of the past; (c) nationalizing states have been more successful at the level of state-building than at the level of nation-building; and (d) in general, the nationalizing states are not likely to become nation-states in the foreseeable future,

the nationalizing states of Eurasia are in a variety of ways ‘incomplete’ and ‘unrealized’, and that their nationalizing elites seek to complete and realize them by a variety of means, including the construction and consolidation of a national identity, the construction of a national history, the construction of national institutions (including a national army, a national economy, a national education system), the construction of a ‘national territory’, the construction of a state language, and so on.

the nationalizing state project is an important factor in the politics of post-communist Eurasia, that this project has been pursued by a variety of actors in different ways, that it has been shaped by a range of factors, and that its impact has been felt in many different areas of social and political life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the processes by which states and societies in post-communist Europe are becoming more ‘national’.
the following question: What are the effects of the nationalizing state on the political and economic development of the new states?
the processes of state‐building, nation‐building and nationalization that are occurring, and are likely to continue occurring, in the post‐communist states of Eurasia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the nationalization of the economy was the most important single factor in the development of the Soviet Union, and that it was the nationalization of agriculture which had the most profound and lasting effect on the Soviet economy as a whole.
nationalizing states are not only a new phenomenon, they are a new kind of state.

the nationalization of states is a complex process, which is not necessarily linear or unilinear, but can be seen as involving a number of interrelated dimensions and phases, and that it is a process which may take a very long time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we try to explain the process of nationalization of the state in a new country.
the article is a conceptual contribution to the study of nationalism, and in particular to the study of the nationalizing states.
the nationalizing states in the new Europe are not the states of nations, but the states of nation-builders.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the process of nationalization is likely to be a long one in many of these new states, with the result that nationalizing states are likely to be a feature of the political landscape in much of post‐communism for many years to come.
nationalization is not just a process of nation‐building, but a process of state‐building as well.
nationalization of the state is a complex, multi‐dimensional, and multi‐level phenomenon.
